title: S-Corp Shareholder Basis: What Form 7203 Tracks
summary: S-corp shareholder basis decides what you can deduct and what gets taxed. See what Form 7203 tracks, how stock and debt basis move, and how to rebuild it.
body_markdown:
## What Is S-Corp Shareholder Basis?


S-corp shareholder basis is a shareholder-level figure that caps your loss deduction and decides how much of a distribution reaches you tax free. It’s your number, not the company’s. Under IRC Section 1366(d)(1), losses and deductions can’t exceed your adjusted stock basis plus the basis of any debt the corporation owes you directly. Under IRC Section 1368(b)(2), a distribution above stock basis is gain from the sale or exchange of property, not a dividend. At indinero we rebuild this schedule for new clients more often than we inherit one.


The IRS is blunt about who owns the record. “It is the shareholder’s responsibility to track a shareholder’s stock and debt basis, not the corporation’s,” says the agency’s page on[S corporation stock and debt basis](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporation-stock-and-debt-basis) . The corporation files Form 1120-S and issues a Schedule K-1. Neither one shows your basis.


Four things to settle first.


- **Basis starts when you acquire the stock.** Contributed cash and property, purchase price, Section 351 carryover basis on an incorporation, or Section 1014 stepped-up value for inherited stock.
- **Basis moves every year the S election is in effect,** whether or not anyone writes it down, and the adjustment lands on the last day of the corporation’s tax year.
- **Basis floors at zero.** The overflow becomes either a suspended deduction or a capital gain.
- **Basis is not the capital account in your books,** and it isn’t the accumulated adjustments account either.


That last one costs the most, so here are the three objects side by side.


Figure Level Governed by What it decides


Tax basis Shareholder, per stock block Section 1367 Loss deductibility and distribution taxability


Book capital account Entity The company’s books, shown on Schedule L Nothing on your Form 1040


Accumulated adjustments account Entity Column (a) of Schedule M-2 Section 1368(c) tiering when accumulated E&P exists


The[Instructions for Form 1120-S](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1120s) say the accumulated adjustments account “is not the same as shareholder basis.” We’re not re-teaching the entity here. If you need the ground floor,[what an S corp is](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-is-an-s-corp/) ,[the Form 2553 election](https://www.indinero.com/blog/irs-form-2553/) , and[the Schedule K-1 itself](https://www.indinero.com/blog/businesses-should-know-about-k-1-forms-tax-filing/) cover it.


## Federal Tax Obligations


Form 7203 is the IRS worksheet that carries S-corp stock and debt basis onto your Form 1040. It attaches to your return, not the corporation’s 1120-S. The current revision is dated December 2022 and remains operative as of October 2026, and it replaced the basis worksheet that used to sit inside the Schedule K-1 instructions.


Attach Form 7203 in any year you:


1. **Claim a deduction for your share of an aggregate loss,** including a loss disallowed last year because of the basis limitation.
2. **Receive a non-dividend distribution.** Dividend distributions don’t count here, and they don’t reduce basis.
3. **Dispose of stock,** whether or not gain is recognized.
4. **Receive a loan repayment from the corporation.**


The form runs three parts and 47 lines. Part I tracks stock basis from the beginning balance through increases, distributions, nondeductible items, allowable losses, and debt basis restoration. Part II gives each shareholder loan its own column. Part III runs loss and deduction items through five columns, ending in the disallowed carryforward. The[Instructions for Form 7203](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i7203) also recommend completing and retaining the form in years with no filing trigger, so the schedule stays continuous.


Basis is also only the first of four gates, ahead of the at-risk rules under Section 465, passive activity loss under Section 469, and the excess business loss limitation under Section 461(l). Clearing basis isn’t the finish line. Our[business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) team runs all four on the same return.


### Stock Basis and Debt Basis


Two running balances, kept apart on purpose. The Form 7203 instructions put it in one line: “Stock basis and debt basis must be figured separately.”


**Stock basis** moves with the K-1 lines you’re actually holding. Increases come from box 1 ordinary income, boxes 2 through 10 separately stated income, box 16A tax-exempt interest, box 16B other tax-exempt income, and box 15C excess depletion. Decreases come from box 1 ordinary loss, boxes 2 through 12 loss and deduction items, box 16C nondeductible expenses, box 16D non-dividend distributions, and box 17R oil and gas depletion.[IRC Section 1367](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1367) is the authority for every one of them. Two decreases get dropped constantly:


- **Box 16C nondeductible expenses.** The 50 percent disallowed half of business meals, fines and penalties, political contributions, and officer life insurance premiums where the company is the beneficiary. They reduce basis even though they never produced a deduction.
- **Section 179.** The corporation’s election passes through and reduces basis in full.[Treas. Reg. 1.179-1(f)(2)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.179-1) requires the reduction even where the Section 179(b) limits stop you from deducting the amount allocated to you.


**Debt basis** is the narrow lane and the most misunderstood part of the subject. Under[Treas. Reg. 1.1366-2(a)(2)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.1366-2) , it exists only for bona fide indebtedness “that runs directly to the shareholder.” A guarantee is nothing. You don’t get basis “merely by guaranteeing a loan or acting as a surety, accommodation party, or in any similar capacity.” Pay on the guaranteed debt and basis arrives, to the extent of that payment. Back-to-back loans do work, where a real debtor-creditor relationship runs from the corporation to you.


Keep open account advances at or under $25,000 at year end.[Treas. Reg. 1.1367-2(a)(2)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.1367-2) defines open account debt as advances not evidenced by separate written instruments whose aggregate outstanding principal doesn’t exceed $25,000 at the close of the corporation’s taxable year. Cross that line and the balance is treated like a separate written instrument for every later year. Restoration is senior too. Under Section 1367(b)(2)(B), a net increase has to restore reduced debt basis before any of it raises stock basis.


### The Annual Ordering Rules


How to calculate S-corp basis is less an arithmetic problem than a sequencing problem. Stock basis adjusts as of the last day of the corporation’s tax year, in a fixed order:


1. **Increase** for income items, including tax-exempt income, and for excess depletion.
2. **Decrease** for non-dividend distributions.
3. **Decrease** for nondeductible, non-capital expenses and depletion.
4. **Decrease** for loss and deduction items.


Distributions come before losses. That single fact is why a profitable-looking company can hand its owner a tax-free distribution and suspend the deduction instead.


Here’s one set of facts run twice. Sole shareholder, stock basis of $40,000 on January 1, 2026. The 2026 Schedule K-1 reports $60,000 of box 1 ordinary income, $90,000 of box 16D distributions, $5,000 of box 16C nondeductible expenses, and a $25,000 Section 179 deduction.


Correct order:


- **Increase.** $40,000 plus $60,000 equals $100,000.
- **Distributions.** $100,000 minus $90,000 equals $10,000. The full $90,000 is tax free. No capital gain.
- **Nondeductible items.** $10,000 minus $5,000 equals $5,000.
- **Losses and deductions.** Only $5,000 of the $25,000 Section 179 is allowed. The other $20,000 is suspended and carries forward indefinitely.
- **Ending stock basis.** Zero.


Wrong order, taking the deductions before the distribution: $40,000 plus $60,000 minus $5,000 minus $25,000 leaves $70,000, so the $90,000 distribution shows $20,000 of capital gain and the full $25,000 Section 179 runs through. Same K-1. Two completely different returns, and only one of them is right.


Push a distribution past basis and the overflow is taxable either way. Had basis opened at $10,000 with $30,000 of income and $65,000 of distributions, $40,000 comes out tax free and the remaining $25,000 is gain from the sale or exchange of property under Section 1368(b)(2), reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D.


One election reorders steps 3 and 4. Reg. 1.1367-1(g) lets you take losses and deductions before nondeductible items, with the unused nondeductible amount carrying over. It needs a statement attached to a timely filed return agreeing to the carryover rule and naming the corporation, and it binds later years unless the IRS consents to revoke.


Suspended amounts aren’t lost.[IRC Section 1366(d)(2)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1366) treats a disallowed loss as incurred by the corporation in the succeeding year with respect to that shareholder, and the loss keeps its character. The carryforward is indefinite, it belongs to you personally, and it dies when you sell the stock.


## State Tax Obligations


Most states follow the federal S election, so state basis tracks the federal number. Three live exceptions break that assumption, and one election moves federal basis in every state that offers it.


**California recognizes the election and taxes the entity anyway.** The[Franchise Tax Board](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/business/types/corporations/s-corporations.html) applies a 1.5 percent tax to the California net income of S corporations with California source income, and the $800 annual minimum franchise tax is owed whether the corporation is active, inactive, operating at a loss, or filing a short-period return. Both consequences run back to basis. The 1.5 percent tax is deductible federally, so it lowers box 1 income and your stock basis with it, and California computes its own net income on Form 100S, so the California basis of the same shares can diverge from the federal figure.


**New York City has no S regime at all.** The city “does not have an S corporation election and does not recognize a New York State S corporation election,” per the Department of Finance’s[General Corporation Tax](https://www.nyc.gov/site/finance/business/business-general-corporation-tax-gct.page) page. Federal S corporations pay the GCT at 8.85 percent of net income allocated to the city, and the corporation pays whichever base produces the largest tax. There is no NYC shareholder basis, because there is no NYC pass-through.


**Tennessee taxes an S corporation as a C corporation.** Excise tax runs at 6.5 percent of net earnings and franchise tax at $0.25 per $100 of net worth. Public Chapter 950, effective May 10, 2024, repealed the alternative property measure of the franchise tax for tax years ending on or after January 1, 2024, leaving net worth as the only base. The Department of Revenue’s[notice 24-05](https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/revenue/documents/notices/fae/24-05fe.pdf) has the mechanics.


**The PTET election moves basis everywhere it exists.**[IRS Notice 2020-75](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-20-75.pdf) treats state income tax imposed on and paid by the corporation as deductible by the corporation in computing its non-separately stated income, not as an item a shareholder takes into account separately. Because the deduction sits inside box 1, every electing shareholder’s federal stock basis fell by their share of the payment. The notice applies to payments made on or after November 9, 2020. California’s elective pass-through entity tax runs at 9.3 percent, extended by Senate Bill 132 through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2031.


A Delaware-incorporated, California-operating, NYC-selling S corp with a Tennessee warehouse has one federal basis schedule and three state regimes that disagree with it. A firm built only for VC-backed Delaware C corps never has to solve that, because a C corp has no shareholder basis limitation to begin with. Multi-state basis work belongs in the same engagement as the rest of the[tax compliance checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/tax-compliance-checklist/) your controller is already working through.


## Entity-Specific Considerations


Basis mechanics follow the tax election, not the state-law wrapper. Indinero serves LLC, S-Corp, C-Corp, multi-entity and non-Delaware companies, and the contrasts below are where that breadth earns its keep.


### An LLC that elected S treatment is on the same hook


Classification follows the election. Members become shareholders for Section 1367 purposes, the capital account in the LLC’s books is still not basis, and Form 7203 is still required the year a trigger hits. The entry point is the basis on the effective date of the election, not the date of formation, which trips up companies that operated as a partnership first. If you’re still choosing the wrapper,[sole proprietorship versus LLC](https://www.indinero.com/blog/sole-proprietorship-vs-llc/) and[types of corporations](https://www.indinero.com/blog/types-of-corporations/) cover that decision.


### Partners get basis for entity debt. Shareholders never do


This is the sharpest contrast in the subject and the reason founders get blindsided. A partner’s outside basis includes a share of partnership-level liabilities under IRC Section 752(a). An S corp shareholder gets nothing for corporate-level debt. Not the bank line, not the SBA loan, not the equipment note, no matter whose personal guarantee sits on the file. The regulation requires indebtedness that runs directly to the shareholder, and a guarantee doesn’t run directly to anyone. So the identical operating loss, in the identical business, is deductible this year inside an LLC taxed as a[partnership](https://www.indinero.com/faq/what-is-a-partnership/) and suspended inside an S corp.


### Four structures that change the answer


- **Stock blocks.** Form 7203 has a stock block line at the top. Shares bought in tranches track block by block, which changes the math on a partial sale.
- **Accumulated E&P from a prior C year.**[IRC Section 1368(c)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1368) tiers the distribution, so a converted company can produce a taxable dividend where a never-C corporation would deliver the same cash tax free.[C corp versus S corp](https://www.indinero.com/blog/c-corp-vs-s-corp/) covers the conversion itself.
- **QSubs and holding structures.** A qualified subchapter S subsidiary is disregarded and its borrowings are corporate debt. A holding company does not manufacture basis.
- **Trust and estate shareholders.** A QSST or ESBT holds the stock, so the schedule lives at the trust level, which is where it disappears during an ownership transition.


## Common Pitfalls


Distributions in excess of basis are the most expensive item on this list, and they’re usually a symptom rather than the cause. Here’s what actually goes wrong, roughly in order of what it costs.


1. **Treating the book capital account as basis.** Different objects at different levels. Changing the books doesn’t change basis.
2. **Counting a personal guarantee as debt basis.** Guarantee alone is nothing. Payment on the guarantee is something.
3. **Dropping box 16C nondeductible expenses.** Skipping them overstates basis year after year, which makes a later distribution look tax free when it isn’t.
4. **Netting shareholder loan repayments against distributions in the ledger.** When the two blur, box 16D is wrong, and every schedule built from it inherits the error.
5. **Letting open account advances pass $25,000 at year end,** which locks that balance into separate-written-instrument treatment for all later years.
6. **Repaying a reduced-basis shareholder note.** Reg. 1.1367-2(d) makes it a recognition event. Capital gain for a formal note, ordinary gain on Form 4797 for open account debt.
7. **Assuming basis increases for the capital gain** you recognized on an excess distribution. It doesn’t.
8. **Forgetting Section 1366(d)(3)** when the S election terminates. The post-termination transition period is the last window to use a suspended loss.


### Rebuilding a schedule nobody ever kept


Most basis work starts here, not with a clean carryforward. The procedure:


1. **Fix the entry point.** Contributed cash and property, purchase price, Section 351 carryover basis, or Section 1014 stepped-up value for inherited stock.
2. **Assemble every Schedule K-1 from year one.** Where the shareholder’s copies are gone, a Form 4506-T wage and income transcript surfaces the K-1 data the IRS received, and Form 4506 pulls full return copies.
3. **Build a four-block table per year** mirroring Form 7203 Part I: increases, distributions, nondeductible items and depletion, then losses and deductions. Carry the ending figure forward and never let it drop below zero.
4. **Hunt the missed lines.** Boxes 16A and 16B tax-exempt income and box 15C excess depletion are increases. Box 16C is a decrease. A spreadsheet built off page one of the K-1 misses all four.
5. **Separate loans from contributions in the ledger history.** Walk every “due to shareholder” and “loan from officer” account back through its postings, then decide year by year which balances were written notes and which were open account debt. That’s[accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) work, not tax work, which is part of why it never gets done.
6. **Handle the closed years.** The AICPA’s Tax Adviser sets out the IRS position from TAM 9304004 and Field Service Advice 200230030 in[S corporation shareholder recomputation of basis](https://www.thetaxadviser.com/issues/2022/feb/s-corporation-shareholder-recomputation-basis/) : losses in excess of basis from closed statute years “must reduce basis in the open statute year after considering the positive adjustments to basis but before considering nondividend distributions.”
7. **Amend the open years** where a loss was claimed without basis, then reconcile the rebuilt figure to Schedule M-2 and Schedule L and document every difference. The differences are the audit defense.


## How Indinero Tracks Shareholder Basis


Basis is built out of bookkeeping detail and used once a year by a tax preparer. That split is why it goes missing.


Every input lives in the ledger. Was the $40,000 the owner wired in March a capital contribution, a written-note loan, or an open account advance. Was the December transfer a distribution or an expense reimbursement. Which meals were 50 percent disallowed, and did they reach box 16C. None of those classifications matter to a bookkeeper closing the month.


All of them decide the basis schedule.


When bookkeeping sits with one vendor and the return with another, the schedule is nobody’s deliverable. The bookkeeper was never asked for it. The preparer needs it and doesn’t have the ledger history to build it, so last year’s number carries forward and the error compounds until a large distribution or a loss year makes it expensive.


Indinero bundles bookkeeping, accounting, tax, and fractional CFO advisory under one monthly engagement, so the ledger that classifies the shareholder advance and the return that reports the limitation come from the same team. In practice:


- A per-shareholder, per-stock-block basis roll-forward maintained inside the monthly close, not reconstructed in filing season.
- A chart of accounts that keeps capital contributions, written-note shareholder loans, open account advances, and distributions apart on purpose, which is what makes box 16D and Form 7203 Part II correct by default.
- A year-end check of planned distributions against projected stock basis before the money moves, so an excess distribution becomes a timing decision instead of a surprise capital gain.
- A year-end review of open account advances against the $25,000 threshold before the balance locks in.
- A completed Form 7203 produced and retained every year, including the years with no filing trigger.
- Reconstruction from prior-year K-1s and IRS transcripts for companies that arrive without a schedule, which is most of them.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up on nearly every basis engagement, from who has to file Form 7203 to what a personal guarantee actually buys you. Short answers below, with the statutory mechanics above if you need the authority behind them.


### Who has to file Form 7203 with their return?


Any S corporation shareholder who claims a loss deduction, takes a non-dividend distribution, disposes of stock, or receives a loan repayment files Form 7203. It attaches to your Form 1040 rather than the corporation’s 1120-S, and the current revision is dated December 2022. The IRS recommends completing and retaining it even in years with no trigger, so indinero produces one annually for S-corp clients to keep the schedule continuous.


### What happens when a distribution is larger than your basis?


A distribution above your stock basis is taxed as capital gain under IRC 1368(b)(2), not as a dividend. The portion within basis comes out tax free and drives basis to zero, and the excess lands on Form 8949 and Schedule D as gain from the sale or exchange of property. Debt basis doesn’t help here, which is why indinero checks planned distributions against projected stock basis before the money moves.


### Can you deduct an S-corp loss that exceeds your basis?


An S-corp loss deduction is capped at your stock basis plus debt basis under IRC 1366(d)(1), so the excess isn’t deductible this year. The disallowed amount is suspended, keeps its character, and carries forward indefinitely until basis is restored by income, a capital contribution, or a new shareholder loan. Basis is also only the first of four gates, ahead of at-risk, passive activity, and excess business loss, and indinero runs all four on the same return.


### Does a shareholder loan to the company create basis?


A shareholder loan creates debt basis in your S corporation when the debt is bona fide and runs directly from the company to you. Debt basis absorbs losses after stock basis hits zero, but it never shelters a distribution. Keep open account advances at or under $25,000 at year end, because Treas. Reg. 1.1367-2(a)(2) otherwise locks that balance into separate-written-instrument treatment for every later year.


### Does personally guaranteeing a company loan give you basis?


A personal guarantee creates no basis in an S corporation, because basis requires an actual economic outlay by the shareholder. This is the sharpest split from a partnership, where IRC 752(a) gives partners basis for a share of entity-level debt. S-corp shareholders get nothing for the bank line or the equipment note, and basis arrives only when you actually pay on the guaranteed debt, to the extent of that payment.


### How do you rebuild a basis schedule nobody ever kept?


Rebuilding an S-corp basis schedule starts with the entry-point basis, then runs every Schedule K-1 from year one through a Form 7203 table. Where the shareholder’s copies are gone, a Form 4506-T transcript surfaces the K-1 data the IRS received, and closed statute years still feed the schedule because basis is cumulative. Indinero reconstructs these from the K-1 history and reconciles the result to Schedule M-2 and Schedule L, documenting every difference.


### Is basis the same number as the capital account in the books?


S-corp shareholder basis and the book capital account are different numbers, one tracked at the shareholder level and one at the entity level. The accumulated adjustments account is a third figure, and the Form 1120-S instructions say outright it is not the same as shareholder basis. Book equity and basis use different ordering and different items, so changing the books never changes basis, and any schedule backed into from the capital account is wrong from the first year forward.
